On a **displacement-time** graph the slope is the **velocity**, and the slope is the
tangent of the angle with the time axis.
**Step 1 — identify what the slope means.**
v = ds/dt = **tan θ** ✓
**Step 2 — write the two velocities.**
v₁ = tan 30° = **1/√3**
v₂ = tan 45° = **1** ✓
**Step 3 — form the ratio.**
v₁ : v₂ = (1/√3) : 1
= **1 : √3** ✓
**A check on the sizes.** 1/√3 = **0·577**, so the first particle is slower - as it must
be, since its graph is less steep ✓ The steeper the displacement-time line, the greater
the speed.
**Why the angle is measured from the time axis.** The x-axis is time and the y-axis is
displacement, so the slope is (change in displacement)/(change in time) ✓ which is the
tangent of the angle the line makes with the **x**-axis.
**What different graphs would mean.**
a **horizontal** line (0°): v = 0, the body at rest ✓
a **steeper** line: faster motion
a **curved** line: changing velocity, that is, acceleration ✓
a line sloping **downward**: motion in the negative direction
**Why a 90° line is impossible.** It would mean infinite velocity - a finite
displacement in zero time ✓ Real displacement-time graphs can approach the vertical but
never reach it.
**A caution about reading angles off a graph.** The numerical slope depends on the
**scales** chosen for the two axes ✓ Doubling the time scale halves the apparent angle
without changing the physics. Such questions assume both axes are drawn to the same
scale, which is implied here.
**The companion graph.** On a **velocity-time** graph the slope is the
**acceleration**, and the **area** under it is the displacement ✓ Keeping straight
which graph is which is half the work in kinematics questions.
**Reading the distractors.** **1 : 1** ✗ would need equal angles. **√3 : 2** ✗ and
**1 : 2** ✗ match no pair of tangents here ✓ tan 30°/tan 45° = 0·577, and only
1 : √3 = 0·577 agrees.
∴ 1 : √3.

The **same force for the same time** gives the same impulse, hence the same **momentum** -
and then the energies go inversely as the masses.
**Step 1 — apply the impulse-momentum theorem.**
Ft = Δp = p ✓
since both start from rest. With F and t the same for both bodies, they acquire
**equal momenta**:
p₁ = p₂ = **Ft** ✓
**Step 2 — express the kinetic energy through momentum.**
E = p²/(2m) ✓
**Step 3 — take the ratio.**
E₁/E₂ = m₂/m₁ ✓
**Why the lighter body gains more energy.** With the same momentum it must move
**faster**, and the energy goes as the **square** of the speed while the momentum goes
only as the first power ✓ The extra speed counts twice over.
**A worked check.** Take F = 10 N, t = 2 s, so p = **20 kg m s⁻¹** for each; let
m₁ = 1 kg and m₂ = 4 kg:
body 1: v = 20 m s⁻¹, E = **200 J**
body 2: v = 5 m s⁻¹, E = **50 J** ✓
ratio E₁/E₂ = 4 = m₂/m₁ ✓
**The distance travelled, for contrast.** With a = F/m, the distance in time t is
s = ½at² = Ft²/(2m), so s ∝ **1/m** ✓ and the work done, Fs, is also proportional to
1/m - consistent with the energy result, as it must be.
**The companion question.** Had the two been pushed through the **same distance**
instead of for the same time, the **work** Fs would be equal and both would gain the
**same energy** ✓ - and then the momenta would go as √m. Which quantity is held common
decides everything.
**A summary of the two cases.**
same **force and time** → equal momenta, E ∝ 1/m ✓
same **force and distance** → equal energies, p ∝ √m ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **m₁/m₂** ✗ inverts the ratio, making the heavier body the
more energetic. **1** ✗ would need equal masses. **√(m₁m₂)/(m₁ + m₂)** ✗ is a
dimensionless combination that appears nowhere in the derivation ✓
∴ m₂/m₁.

In a dispersive medium the refractive index is **largest for violet**, so violet travels
**slowest** and red fastest.
**Step 1 — relate speed to refractive index.**
v = c/n ✓
so the colour with the **smallest** n travels **fastest**.
**Step 2 — recall how n varies with colour.** For ordinary glass,
violet (400 nm): n ≈ **1·53**
red (700 nm): n ≈ **1·51** ✓
The index **falls** as the wavelength grows - normal dispersion.
**Step 3 — conclude.** Red has the smallest n and therefore the **greatest speed** in
the glass ✓
**The speeds, worked out.**
violet: 3 x 10⁸/1·53 = **1·96 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹**
red: 3 x 10⁸/1·51 = **1·99 x 10⁸ m s⁻¹** ✓ about 1·3% faster.
**Why all colours travel together in vacuum.** There c = 1/√(µ₀ε₀), with no reference
to frequency ✓ Dispersion is entirely a property of the **medium**, arising from the
response of its electrons, which depends on frequency.
**Why "incident normally" matters here.** At normal incidence there is **no bending**,
so the colours do not separate in direction ✓ Only their **speeds** differ inside the
glass - which is exactly what the question asks about. Had the light entered
obliquely, a spectrum would also appear.
**Cauchy's formula.**
n = A + B/λ² ✓
so n decreases as λ increases - a steady trend across the visible range, steepest at the
blue end.
**Why a prism makes a spectrum.** Violet, being most slowed, is bent **most**, and red
least ✓ The separation comes from the same index variation that controls the speeds
here.
**Why the sky's rainbow has red on the outside.** Refraction in a raindrop separates the
colours by the same mechanism, and the geometry puts red at the larger deviation
angle ✓
**Reading the distractors.** "**Violet travels faster**" ✗ reverses the index order.
"**All colours the same speed**" ✗ is true in **vacuum**, not in glass. "**Yellow
fastest**" ✗ singles out a middle wavelength for no reason ✓
∴ red light travels faster than other colours.

Use I = n A e v_d and solve for the drift speed.
**Step 1 — state the relation.**
I = n A e v_d ✓
with n the free-electron density, A the cross-section and e the electronic charge.
**Step 2 — rearrange.**
v_d = I/(n A e) ✓
**Step 3 — substitute.** Taking the area as **2 x 10⁻⁶ m²**:
v_d = 2/[(5 x 10²⁶)(2 x 10⁻⁶)(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹)]
**Step 4 — evaluate the denominator step by step.**
(5 x 10²⁶)(2 x 10⁻⁶) = **10²¹**
10²¹ x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹ = **160** ✓
**Step 5 — divide.**
v_d = 2/160
= **1/80 m s⁻¹** ✓
**How slow that is.** 1/80 m s⁻¹ = **1·25 cm s⁻¹** ✓ An electron would take over a
minute to crawl a single metre along the wire.
**Why the lamp lights instantly, then.** The **electric field** is established along the
wire at nearly the speed of light ✓ Every electron in the circuit starts drifting almost
at once - the current begins everywhere simultaneously, even though each individual
electron moves at a snail's pace.
**The contrast with thermal speed.** Random thermal motion is about **10⁵ m s⁻¹**, some
**ten million times** faster than the drift ✓ The drift is a tiny systematic bias
superimposed on violent random motion.
**Why n is so large.** 5 x 10²⁶ free electrons per cubic metre means roughly one per
atom ✓ It is this enormous density that lets a huge current flow with so slow a drift.
**A note on the printed area.** The question writes "2 x 10⁶ m²", which would be a
cross-section of two square kilometres ✓ The intended value is plainly **2 x 10⁻⁶ m²**,
that is 2 mm² - a typical wire - and that is what the options are built on.
**Reading the distractors.** **1/40**, **1/32** and **1/16 m s⁻¹** ✗ correspond to
denominators of 80, 64 and 32 rather than 160 ✓ The arithmetic hinges on
(5 x 10²⁶)(2 x 10⁻⁶)(1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹) = 160.
∴ 1/80 ms⁻¹.

The one-second interval is the **time to reach the top**, which fixes the launch speed.
**Step 1 — read the condition.** The next ball is thrown exactly when the previous one's
velocity reaches zero - that is, when it reaches its **highest point** ✓ Since the
interval is one second,
time to the top = **1 s** ✓
**Step 2 — find the launch speed.**
v = u − gt, with v = 0 at t = 1 s:
u = gt = (10)(1)
= **10 m s⁻¹** ✓
**Step 3 — find the height.**
h = u²/(2g)
= 100/20
= **5 m** ✓
**A check by the other route.**
h = ut − ½gt² = 10(1) − 5(1) = **5 m** ✓
**The pattern in the air.** At the instant a ball is thrown, the previous one is at the
**top** (5 m), and the one before that is **back in the thrower's hand** ✓ The total
flight time is 2 s, so at any moment there are exactly **two** balls aloft.
**Why only the time matters.** The height follows from the launch speed, and the launch
speed from the time to the top ✓ Neither the mass of the ball nor the thrower's
strength enters.
**A useful pair of relations.**
time up = time down = **u/g** ✓
total flight time = **2u/g** ✓
maximum height = **u²/2g** = ½g(time up)² ✓
Here the last form is quickest: ½(10)(1)² = 5 m.
**What a longer interval would give.** A 2 s interval needs u = 20 m s⁻¹ and gives
h = **20 m** ✓ The height goes as the **square** of the interval, so doubling the
interval quadruples the height.
**Reading the distractors.** **10 m** ✗ would need u = 14·1 m s⁻¹ and 1·41 s to the
top. **20 m** ✗ needs 2 s. **7·5 m** ✗ needs 1·22 s ✓ Only 5 m corresponds to exactly
one second of rise.
∴ 5 m.

Find the acceleration from the specific charge, then use v² = 2as.
**Step 1 — find the acceleration.**
a = eE/m = (e/m)E
= (1·8 x 10¹¹)(1 x 10⁴)
= **1·8 x 10¹⁵ m s⁻²** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the kinematic relation.** The electron starts from rest:
v² = 2as
= 2(1·8 x 10¹⁵)(2 x 10⁻²)
= **7·2 x 10¹³** ✓
**Step 3 — take the square root.**
v = √(7·2 x 10¹³)
= √(72 x 10¹²)
= 8·49 x 10⁶
≈ **8·5 x 10⁶ m s⁻¹** ✓
**Why the specific charge is enough.** The acceleration is eE/m, which contains only
the **ratio** e/m ✓ Neither the charge nor the mass is needed separately - a convenience
that comes up repeatedly in electron-beam problems.
**A check through energy.** The work done is eEs, so
½mv² = eEs
v² = 2(e/m)Es = 2(1·8 x 10¹¹)(10⁴)(2 x 10⁻²) = **7·2 x 10¹³** ✓ the same.
**The energy in electron volts.**
eV = eEs, with Es = 10⁴ x 2 x 10⁻² = **200 V**
so the electron gains **200 eV** ✓ and the useful shortcut v = 5·93 x 10⁵√V gives
5·93 x 10⁵ x √200 = **8·4 x 10⁶ m s⁻¹** ✓ agreeing.
**How fast that is.** 8·5 x 10⁶ m s⁻¹ is about **2·8%** of the speed of light ✓ fast,
but comfortably non-relativistic: the relativistic correction here is under 0·1%, so
the classical formula is sound.
**How enormous the acceleration is.** 1·8 x 10¹⁵ m s⁻² is some **10¹⁴ times g** ✓ which
is why gravity is always ignored in electron-beam calculations.
**Reading the distractors.** **0·85 x 10⁶** ✗ and **0·425 x 10⁶** ✗ are ten and twenty
times too small - they come from a slip in the powers of ten. **1·6 x 10⁶** ✗ matches no
step ✓ Checking √(7·2 x 10¹³) by writing it as √(72) x 10⁶ = 8·49 x 10⁶ keeps the
exponent straight.
∴ 8.5 × 10⁶.

The stopping distance under a constant retarding force goes as the **square** of the
initial speed.
**Step 1 — apply the work-energy theorem.** All the kinetic energy is removed by the
retarding force over the stopping distance:
½mu² = F s ✓
so
**s = mu²/(2F)**
**Step 2 — see the dependence.** With m and F fixed,
**s ∝ u²** ✓
**Step 3 — double the speed.**
s₂/s₁ = (2u/u)²
= **4**
**s₂ = 4s₁** ✓
**The kinematic route.** With deceleration a = F/m,
v² = u² − 2as, and v = 0 at the stop:
s = u²/(2a) ✓ the same quadratic dependence, with no mention of energy.
**Why doubling the speed quadruples the distance.** The vehicle has **four times** the
kinetic energy, and the same force removes energy at the same rate per metre ✓ so four
times the distance is needed.
**The road-safety consequence.** This is the single most important fact about braking ✓
A car at 60 km/h needs four times the braking distance of one at 30 km/h, not twice -
and at 90 km/h, nine times. Stopping distances in the Highway Code follow exactly this
rule.
**A worked instance.** With m = 1000 kg and F = 5000 N:
at 10 m s⁻¹: s = 1000(100)/10000 = **10 m**
at 20 m s⁻¹: s = 1000(400)/10000 = **40 m** ✓ four times.
**What about the stopping time?** That goes only as **u**:
t = u/a ✓ so doubling the speed **doubles** the time but **quadruples** the distance.
The two scale differently, which is worth keeping straight.
**The real-world addition.** Total stopping distance = **thinking distance** +
**braking distance** ✓ The thinking distance is proportional to u, the braking distance
to u² - so the quadratic term dominates at speed.
**Reading the distractors.** **s₂ = 2s₁** ✗ assumes a linear dependence - the commonest
and most dangerous misconception. **s₂ = s₁** ✗ ignores the change entirely, and
**s₂ = s₁/2** ✗ has it backwards ✓
∴ s₂ = 4s₁.
